To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the TSEB is an excellent tool for calculating E and T, but it requires the Penman-Montith formulation for the energy balance equation to account for the impact of VPD; (2) TSC ET and TSC TEMP are equally valid time-scaling methods for the TSEB; (3) T R measurement time is not very critical, although morning T R measurement times should be avoided.

the TSEB model using the Penman–Monteith equation (TSEB-PM) is a better model for calculating E, T, ET, and their partitioning than the TSEB using the Priestley–Taylor equation (TSEBT-PT) in the semiarid environment of Bushland, TX; and the TSEBT-PM is a good model for calculating E and T, but the model is less accurate for ET.

the TSEB is an effective method to calculate E, ET, and T for irrigated cotton in a semiarid environment, and the use of the Priestley Taylor equation in the TSEB resulted in overestimation of E and underestimation of T, whereas the Penman Monteith equation greatly improved the agreement with measured E, T, ET, and ETc.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the TSEB should be modified to use the Penman-Montieth formulation for calculating E, T, or ET, and that TSC TEMP is a better time scaling method for calculating E or T, and TSC ET is a better method for calculating ET.

(i) T R is an excellent surrogate for surface temperature, (ii) T R can be measured at any convenient time during the day, (iii) T R can also be measured at any time during the previous night, and (iv) the Penman-Montheith formulation is a much better choice for TSEB than the Priestley-Talyor formulation.
